title: Registri Epistolarum
author: Gregory the Great
source: Translated by Claude from tmp1291.tmp1291.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: Prima itaque episiolae vestrae frons gravem vos pati persecutionem innotuit. Quse quidem persecutio dum non rationabiliter sutinetur, nequaquam proficit ad salatem. Nam nulli fas est retributionem praemiorum ex. spectare pro culpa. Debetis enim scire, sicut beatus Cyprianus ait, quia b martyrem nou facit paena, sed causa. Hum igitur ita sit, incongruum nimis est de ea vos, quam dicitis, persecutione gloriari, per quam vos constat ad aeterna praemia minime provehi.
passages.english: So the very opening of your letter made known that you are suffering a heavy persecution. But this persecution, so long as it is not endured for a reasonable cause, does nothing at all to advance [your] salvation. For no one may rightly expect the repayment of rewards for a fault. You ought to know, as the blessed Cyprian says, that it is not the punishment that makes a martyr, but the cause. Since, then, this is so, it is quite unfitting for you to glory in what you call persecution, through which it is clear that you are by no means being carried forward to eternal rewards.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (episiolae, Quse, sutinetur, salatem, nou, Hum = Cum). Stray 'b' is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Altestantur huic eximiae doctrinae tuae saneii antiqui Patres, dociores, defensoresque Ecclesiae, Hilarius, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Gregorius Nazianzenus; bi omnes testimonium tibi praebent, sicut apostolis præbuerunt prophetæ. Hilarius sanctus dicit, exponens verba Apostoli doctoris gentium : « c Ita etenim quæ propriae disciplinae et morum sunt, ad sacerdotii meritum utilia esse significat, si etiam haec 611 quae ad docendæ ac tuendæ fi lei scientiam necessario sunt, inter reliqua non deerunt; quia non staiim boni atque utilis sacerdotis est, aut tantummodo scienter agere, aut tantummodo scienter prædicare, cum et innocens tantum sui sufficiat si doctus sit, et doctus nisi doctrina vivendo. Attestatur huic libro tuo sanctus Ambrosius in illis libris quos fecit de Officiis. Attestatur sanctus Augustinus, dicens : a In actione non amandus est honor in hac vita,sine [Lege sive] potentia, quoniam omnia vana suh sole; sed opus ipsum quod per eumdem honorcm vel poteMtiam fit, si recte atque utiliter fit, id est ut valeat ad eam salutem subditorum, quæ secundum Deum est... Propter quod ait Apostolus: Qui episcopatum desiderat, opus bonum desiderat.Exponere voluit quid sit episcopus [Forte episcopatus], quia nomen est operis, non honoris. Graecum est enim, et inde ductum vocabulum , quod ille qui præficitur eis quibus praeficitur superintendit, curam scilicet eorum gerens, episcopus [Forte episcopalus] quippe intentio est.
passages.english: The holy ancient Fathers, teachers and defenders of the Church, bear witness to this outstanding teaching of yours: Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory of Nazianzus; all these give testimony to you, as the prophets gave it to the apostles. Saint Hilary, expounding the words of the Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, says: "For thus he indicates that the things which belong to personal discipline and conduct are useful for the merit of the priesthood, if also those things which are necessary for the knowledge of teaching and defending the faith are not lacking among the rest; because it is not at once [the mark] of a good and useful priest either only to act knowingly or only to preach knowingly, since even the innocent man suffices only for himself unless he is learned, and the learned man [suffices nothing] unless [he supports his] teaching by living." Saint Ambrose bears witness to this book of yours in those books which he wrote On Duties. Saint Augustine bears witness, saying: "In action, honour or power in this life is not to be loved, since all things under the sun are vain; but the work itself which is done through that honour or power, if it is done rightly and usefully, that is, so that it avails for that salvation of those under [one's charge] which is according to God... For this reason the Apostle says: Whoever desires the episcopate desires a good work. He wished to explain what the episcopate is, because it is the name of a work, not of an honour. For it is Greek, and the word is derived from the fact that he who is set over others oversees those over whom he is set, that is, bearing care for them; for episcopus [means] attention."
passages.notes: Following the edition's suggested readings (sive for sine; episcopatus for episcopus). The last clause of the Hilary quotation is elliptical and seems defective ('et doctus nisi doctrina vivendo'); bracketed words supply the probable sense. The final 'episcopus' likely should be the Greek episkopē ('oversight').

passages.original: Hortatur Augustini socios ut cœptum in Angliam per-agant iter. Augustino quem illis abbatem constituitobediant.
passages.english: He urges Augustine's companions to complete the journey they have begun to England, [and] to obey Augustine, whom he has appointed their abbot.

passages.original: Ut Virgilium Arelatensem de pensionibus Romam mittendis urgeat, et Candidum habeatcommen- datum.
passages.english: That he should urge Virgilius of Arles about sending the rents to Rome, and should hold Candidus commended.

passages.original: Ut Augustino in Angliam eunti et Candido rectori pa- trimonii tuitionem et auxilium impendat.
passages.english: That he should give protection and help to Augustine, who is going to England, and to Candidus, the rector of the patrimony.

passages.original: Sed quia ex annotalione hæretici Codicis, qui ad me ex regia urbe transmissus est, agnovi per hoc quod quædam capitula cathol ca cum hæreticis fuerant reprehensa quia quidam illam Ephesinam primam synodum in eadem urbe exisrimant, quæ quondam ab haereticis traditur esse composita, omnino necesse est ut charitas vestra eamdem synodum apud sanctam A lexandrinam atque Ant:ochenam Ecclesiam requirat, et qualiter in vcritale habeatur inveniat. Vel, si placet, hinc dirigimus quæ ab antiquitate servata in scriniis habemus. Illa enim synodus quae sub primae Ephesinae imagine facta est, quædam in se oblata capitula asserit approbata, quae sunt Coelestii atque Pelagii praedicamenla. Et cum Cœlestius atque Pelngius in ea synodo sint damnati, quomodo poterant illa capitula recipi, quorum damnabantur auctores?
passages.english: But since, from the annotation of a heretical codex which was sent to me from the royal city, I learned that certain catholic chapters had been censured along with heretical ones, because some in that same city take to be the first synod of Ephesus that [synod] which is reported to have been put together long ago by heretics, it is altogether necessary that your charity seek out that same synod at the holy Church of Alexandria and of Antioch, and find how it is held in truth. Or, if you please, we will send from here what we have, preserved from antiquity, in our archives. For that synod which was held under the guise of the first [synod] of Ephesus asserts that certain chapters presented to it were approved, which are the doctrines of Caelestius and Pelagius. And since Caelestius and Pelagius were condemned in that synod, how could those chapters be accepted whose authors were being condemned?
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently: annotalione = annotatione, cathol ca = catholica, exisrimant = existimant, A lexandrinam = Alexandrinam, Ant:ochenam = Antiochenam, vcritale = veritate, praedicamenla = praedicamenta, Pelngius = Pelagius. The "royal city" is presumably Constantinople. The sentence beginning "because some in that same city…" is somewhat loosely constructed in the Latin; the sense is that a spurious synod was being taken for the genuine first council of Ephesus.

passages.original: Quid d ergo dicis de Pascha 21 aut 22 lunæ quod jam ( tua [Iui in Ms.] tamen pace dictum sit) non esse Pascha, nimirum 'enebrosum a multis comp-o- batur e calcalenteris? Non latet enim, ut credo, efficaciam tuam, quantum Anatolius, miræ. doctrinæ vir, ut sanctus ait Hieronymus, cujus Eusebius Caesariensis episcopus in Ecclesiastica excerpta inseruit Historia, et sanctus Hieronymus in suo hoc idem de Pascha opus collauda vit catalogo, de hac lunae ætate vituperando disputet; qui contra Gallicanos f Rimarios, de Pascha, ut ait, 1037 errantes, horrendam intulit sententiam , dicens : Certe [Ms.
passages.english: What then do you say about Easter on the 21st or 22nd day of the moon, which (by your leave be it said) is not Easter, being plainly shown by many calculators to be dark? For it is not hidden, I believe, from your efficiency how much Anatolius, a man of wonderful learning, as Saint Jerome says—excerpts from whom Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, inserted in his Ecclesiastical History, and whom Saint Jerome praised in his Catalogue for this same work on Easter—argues in censure of this age of the moon; who against the Gallican calculators, erring about Easter, as he says, brought a dreadful judgement, saying: Certainly [Ms.
passages.notes: Text garbled: 'enebrosum a multis comp-o- batur e calcalenteris' read as tenebrosum... comprobatur a calculatoribus; 'Rimarios' uncertain, perhaps for calculatores/numerarios. The passage breaks off mid-quotation with an editorial manuscript note.

passages.original: De Innocentii præfectura gaudet ex dilectione; dolet ex gravitate muneris, quam illi æternæ mercedis occasionem fieri peroplat. Factas indicat cum Langobardorum rege inducias. Suos in Job postulanti laudat Augustini libros. De protecto Romanae Ecclesiæ patrimonio gratias agit.
passages.english: He rejoices out of love at Innocent's prefecture; he grieves at the weight of the office, which he earnestly wishes may become for him an occasion of eternal reward. He reports the truce made with the king of the Lombards. He praises Augustine's books to [Innocent], who asks for his own [books] on Job. He gives thanks for the protection of the patrimony of the Roman Church.
passages.notes: The sentence on Job is compressed: Innocent asked for Gregory's work on Job, and Gregory commends Augustine's books instead.

passages.original: Ita autem doctrina vestra per omnia Latinis Patritius concordavit, ut mirum mihi non esset quod in diversis linguis Spiritus non fuerit diversus. Nam hoc quod de ficulnea dixistis, in eo ser.su proprie beatus Augustinus loquitur, quia curn evangelista subjunxit : Nondum enim erat tempus ficorum (Marc. xi, 13), aperte cognoscitur quod per ficum Dominus in synagoga fructum qucesierat, quae folia legis habuit, sed fructum operis non habebat. Non euim poterat Creator omnium nescire quia fructum ficus non habuit;
passages.english: Your teaching has so agreed in all things with the Latin Fathers that it was no wonder to me that in different languages the Spirit was not different. For what you said about the fig tree, the blessed Augustine speaks of in that very sense, since when the evangelist added: For it was not yet the season for figs (Mark 11:13), it is plainly recognised that through the fig the Lord had sought fruit in the synagogue, which had the leaves of the law but did not have the fruit of works. For the Creator of all could not fail to know that the fig tree had no fruit;
